blocks.text: 4-bit quantization represents each model weight using just 4 bits, only 16 possible distinct values per weight, an aggressive but carefully engineered precision reduction that forms the specific foundation QLoRA relies on to fit large models into limited GPU memory.

This topic focuses on 4-bit quantization specifically, building on the general quantization ideas from the previous topic and setting up the NF4 and double quantization techniques covered in the next two topics of this module.
1. What 4-Bit Quantization Means Specifically

blocks.alt: A 32-bit weight gets reduced down to a 4-bit weight

blocks.text: Where the general quantization topic covered reducing precision broadly, 4-bit quantization is the specific, extreme case, using just 4 bits per weight, enough to represent only 16 distinct possible values, a dramatic reduction from the millions of distinct values 32-bit precision can represent.
2. From 16 or 32 Bits Down to 4

blocks.alt: 32 bits steps down through 16 bits to 4 bits

blocks.text: Going from 32-bit precision to 4-bit precision is not a small step, it is an eightfold reduction in bits per weight, the most aggressive precision level commonly used in practical fine-tuning workflows, only made viable by the careful value mapping techniques covered later in this topic and the next.
3. The Memory Savings, Worked Out

blocks.alt: Full precision memory for a 7 billion parameter model is compared against its 4-bit equivalent

blocks.text: A model with 7 billion parameters stored at 32-bit precision requires roughly 28 gigabytes of memory just for the weights themselves. The same model quantized to 4-bit precision requires roughly 3.5 gigabytes, an eightfold reduction that can be the difference between a model fitting on available hardware or not fitting at all.

code.content:
# The memory reduction from full precision to 4-bit
def memory_gb(param_count_billions, bits_per_param):
    return (param_count_billions * 1e9 * bits_per_param) / 8 / 1e9

print(memory_gb(7, 32))  # roughly 28 GB
print(memory_gb(7, 4))   # roughly 3.5 GB

blocks.text: 4. How 4-Bit Values Represent a Wider Range

blocks.alt: Only 16 possible levels requires careful value mapping

blocks.text: With only 16 distinct values available, mapping real weight values, which can span a wide continuous range, onto those 16 discrete levels requires careful design, a naive uniform spacing wastes precision on rarely occurring values while a more thoughtful mapping, covered directly in the next NF4 topic, allocates precision where the actual weight distribution needs it most.
5. Quality Impact of Going This Low

blocks.alt: Some quality loss is traded off against massive memory savings

blocks.text: 4-bit quantization does introduce measurable quality loss compared to full precision, though careful quantization schemes, particularly NF4 covered next, have shown this loss can be kept surprisingly small for many practical fine-tuning purposes, especially when only the frozen base model is quantized while the actively trained LoRA matrices remain at higher precision.

blocks.text: 6. 4-Bit Quantization as the Foundation of QLoRA

QLoRA specifically quantizes the frozen base model down to 4-bit precision, freeing up enough memory to train LoRA matrices on top, a combination that makes it possible to fine-tune models on a single consumer GPU that would otherwise require far more expensive, specialized hardware at full precision.
7. Dequantization During Computation

blocks.alt: 4-bit stored weights get dequantized on the fly for computation

blocks.text: Weights stored at 4-bit precision are not directly usable for the numerically sensitive matrix multiplications a forward pass requires, so they get dequantized, converted back to a higher precision, on the fly during computation, keeping the memory savings from storage while still performing the actual math at a precision level that produces reliable results.

blocks.title: Storage precision and computation precision can differ
blocks.content: A weight can be stored at 4-bit precision to save memory, then temporarily expanded to a higher precision just for the moment it is actually used in a calculation, a pattern central to how QLoRA achieves both memory savings and reasonable training quality.

blocks.text: 8. When 4-Bit Is Worth the Precision Loss

blocks.alt: A 4-bit base model pairs with LoRA matrices trained at higher precision

blocks.text: 4-bit quantization is most clearly worth its precision cost specifically when it is the difference between a fine-tuning run fitting on available hardware or not fitting at all, since the LoRA matrices being actively trained still operate at a higher precision, limiting how much the quantized base model precision loss actually propagates into the final fine-tuned quality.
9. Practical Tools That Support 4-Bit Quantization

Several widely used fine-tuning libraries, covered in more depth in the Fine-Tuning Frameworks module later in this course, provide built in support for loading a base model directly in 4-bit quantized form, handling the quantization and dequantization details so a practitioner does not need to implement the underlying numeric mapping from scratch.
Worked Example

A developer wants to fine-tune a 7 billion parameter model on a single consumer GPU with 8 gigabytes of memory, nowhere near enough for full precision fine-tuning, which would need well over 28 gigabytes just for the base model weights.

Loading the base model in 4-bit quantized form shrinks its memory footprint to roughly 3.5 gigabytes, leaving enough room for the LoRA matrices and training overhead to fit comfortably within the available 8 gigabytes, turning an otherwise impossible fine-tuning run into a practical one.
Common Mistakes

items: Assuming 4-bit quantization applies to the actively trained LoRA matrices as well as the frozen base, when typically only the base is quantized
Underestimating the memory savings 4-bit quantization actually provides, and reaching for far more expensive hardware than necessary
Not understanding that dequantization happens on the fly during computation, mistakenly assuming the model computes at 4-bit precision throughout
Choosing 4-bit quantization for a task where full precision hardware was actually available and unnecessary quality loss was introduced

blocks.text: Practice

For a model size of your choosing, calculate the memory footprint at 4-bit precision, then compare it against the memory available on a GPU you have access to or are considering, confirming whether 4-bit quantization would make a fine-tuning run on that hardware feasible.
Key Takeaway

4-bit quantization represents each weight using only 16 possible values, delivering an eightfold memory reduction compared to full precision, and combined with dequantization on the fly during computation and LoRA training kept at higher precision, it forms the specific foundation that makes QLoRA practical on hardware that could never handle full precision fine-tuning.
